newsitem.title: USA: CSX to acquire Conrail in merger of rail giants.
newsitem.headline: CSX to acquire Conrail in merger of rail giants.

text.p: CSX Corp. said on Tuesday it was acquiring Conrail Inc. for about $8.4 billion in a merger that will create a rail freight giant dominating the eastern United States.

The deal sent Conrail's stock soaring due to the healthy premium on its share price, while CSX sagged on what analysts said were company forecasts the deal would not be profitable until the second year after its expected completion in late 1997.

The merger, CSX Chairman John Snow told a telephone news conference, "will enable us, we are confident, to regain substantial traffic from the highways and produce much higher rates of growth for the combined company than either of us have experienced before."

The combination will create a dominant freight transportation company with annual revenues of more than $14 billion, offering domestic and international customers rail, container-shipping, barge, and intermodal transportation services.

It also marks another milestone in the comeback of Conrail, which was formed by the federal government in 1976 from the combination of six bankrupt northeastern U.S. railroads. The government sold its stock in the firm to the public in 1987.

A new holding company for the combined firm will be headquartered in Philadelphia, where Conrail is based. A headquarters location for the rail operation has not been decided. CSX is based in Richmond, Va., and its rail operation is based in Jacksonville, Florida.

The newly created transportation system will offer extensive rail service in 22 eastern states over 29,645 miles (47,600 km) of track covering a territory from Chicago, Boston and New York to Miami and New Orleans.

Key to the deal is that it gives the combined firm continuous north-south routes, allowing it to more effectively compete with trucks, especially along busy Interstate 95 on the economically powerful East Coast.
"Many shippers are going to be attracted back to rail," said Conrail Chairman David LeVan.
In addition to possibly relieving traffic on Interstate 95 and other highways, the merger will free up track in the Northeast corridor, which Conrail now pays passenger rail service Amtrak to use.

Amtrak spokesman Rob Borella said the deal would have no immediate impact on operations, but any reduction in freight traffic could improve on-time performance. He said he did not know how much money Amtrak could lose in Conrail payments as the rail switches to CSX track.
Conrail and CSX project increased traffic will boost operating income by $200 million annually.

The companies also forecast another $350 million in cost savings, and said there would be "some job losses." Officials said they could not estimate the number of losses, and that in the long term, the company would grow.
Under the deal, Conrail shareholders will receive a combination of cash and CSX shares valued at about $92.50 per Conrail share -- a big premium over the stock's closing price of $71 on Monday.
Conrail shares closed at $85.125, up $14.125, on the New York Exchange. CSX shares were down $2.75 at $46.75.
Analysts said the deal's level of success will likely depend on how much competitive access the merged firm must grant along its key north-south routes, analysts said.
Asked whether the deal was worth the premium, Prudential Securities analyst Brian Routledge said earlier rail mergers have shown that significant benefits can be gained.

"How quickly they realise those benefits will depend on how much access they have to give up to competing railroads in the regulatory process, and we won't know that until probably late next year," Routledge said.

Approval from the federal Surface Transportation Board is required for the merger to take place. Analysts said approval was likely, but the board would probably seek to make sure there was a competitive environment.

Norfolk Southern Corp -- which was in late 1994 rumoured to be in merger talks with Conrail -- on Tuesday said the proposed merger raised concerns regarding the transportation system and shipping public.
Snow said he and LeVan intended to "sit down with our counterparts at Norfolk Southern...and see if we can't accommodate their concerns."
CSX and Conrail said in announcing their merger that they were willing to grant competitive access on track where the two firms are now the only competitors.
Some grain shippers in the region to be served by the combined firm said the merger would open up markets, but also expressed caution about its affect on rates.

"It's going to make a bigger market for shippers and receivers, but any time two competitors merge, you run the risk of higher freight rates," said one grain merchant in the southeastern United States.
